title: Man dragged into jail cell
article: A man who died after spending a night in the Maple Ridge drunk tank was dragged into the concrete cell on a blanket.
Sgt. Roland Pierschke and a jail guard got no assistance from Ian Alexander Young as they lugged him down a corridor.
"He appeared to be sleepy and intoxicated," Const. Jodi Lymburner told an inquest investigating Young's death on Wednesday.
"He grumbled responses when he was moved."

Young was taken into custody by Lymburner on Oct. 17, 2008 after a passerby found him lying on the side of the road in Hammond, seemingly intoxicated. Young had been drinking at the By Bailey Pub before he was found.
Almost eight hours later, during regular cell checks at Ridge Meadows RCMP detachment, officers found the man breathing, but non-responsive.
The 55-year-old was transported to Ridge Meadows Hospital, where doctors determined he needed medical intervention.
The man was then rushed to Royal Columbian Hospital, where he underwent surgery.
Young died two days later in hospital from a head injury.
Paramedics who dealt with Young testified he smelled of alcohol and was unsteady. He had an abrasion on his head.
They said Young refused medical treatment at least three times and signed a release form.
Still concerned for his well-being, one of the paramedics walked down Waresley Street to Young's house.
Ron Henderson testified he spoke with Young's wife Karen telling her that her husband was found intoxicated, lying on the street.
Henderson told her they couldn't leave her husband on the street and would most likely be transporting him to RCMP cells.
Young's wife did not want her drunk husband at home because her young daughter was having a sleep over.
Although paramedics were worried about Young's condition, they called police and struggled to load him into a cruiser.
Young was eventually put on a stretcher and pulled by both paramedics into the car.
Paramedics testified they told Const. Lymburner that Young needed to be monitored.
But Lymburner said she received no such instructions from paramedics.
"They told me they had no concerns for him," she said.
Once inside the drunk tank, the inquest heard police repeatedly violated policy that required officers to rouse inmates, make sure they respond and never assume inmates were "sleeping it off."
A card detailing "rouseability" checks is posted in every jail cell.
Young was never checked when placed in the drunk tank or throughout the night, despite concerns expressed by the jail guard on duty to the Sgt. Pierschke, the RCMP officer in charge of the watch.
Young was found the next morning after a corporal took over command, with a clear fluid, tinged with blood, oozing from his head.
RCMP poked him in the stomach with their boots to wake him and called paramedics when he didn't wake up.
A man who shared the cell with Young on the night in question told the inquest not much has changed.
Willem Vanderbom, who is battling an alcohol addiction, is intimate with the drunk tank, having spent more than 40 nights in it over the past three years.
He said cell checks improved for a short time after Young's death, but have since dwindled, with officers and guards only checking on inmates through a small window.
"Maple Ridge is fairly rough," said Vanderbom, who got a black eye during his last stint in the drunk tank two weeks ago.
"They hit you with torches. They re-broke my collar bone. I've been in Nanaimo, Coquitlam, New West. All those places they treat you with dignity."
Presiding coroner Vincent Stancato and a jury will hear evidence in order to determine the facts surrounding Young's death until Friday.
The jury will then have the opportunity to make recommendations aimed at preventing deaths under similar circumstances in the future.
The inquest is a fact-finding process that can't make any finding have legal consequence.
